modules.title: Introduction to the Human Brain
modules.summary: Meet the four major divisions of the brain and learn how to orient yourself in 3D.

steps.title: Welcome
steps.text: This is a 3D model of an adult human brain built from the BodyParts3D anatomical database. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom. You are looking from the front (anterior view): the patient's left is on your right.

steps.title: The cerebrum
steps.text: The cerebrum is the large, folded upper part, made of two hemispheres. Its surface — the cerebral cortex — is folded into ridges (gyri) and grooves (sulci).

steps.title: The cerebellum
steps.text: Tucked under the back of the cerebrum is the cerebellum, which coordinates movement and balance.

steps.title: The brainstem
steps.text: The brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord and controls vital functions such as breathing and heart rate.

steps.title: The diencephalon
steps.text: Deep in the centre, hidden by the hemispheres, is the diencephalon — including the thalamus and hypothalamus. We make the cortex transparent to see it.

quiz.q: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and smooth movement?
quiz.explain: The cerebellum coordinates timing and accuracy of movement and balance.

quiz.q: In an anterior view of the brain, the patient's left hemisphere appears on…
quiz.explain: Facing the patient, their left is on your right.

modules.title: Understanding the Cerebral Lobes
modules.summary: Explore frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes and the hidden insula.

steps.title: Frontal lobe
steps.text: The frontal lobe extends forward from the central sulcus. Its precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex; further forward, prefrontal cortex supports planning and self-control.

steps.title: Parietal lobe
steps.text: Behind the central sulcus, the parietal lobe begins with the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) and integrates information for spatial awareness.

steps.title: Temporal lobe
steps.text: Below the lateral fissure, the temporal lobe handles hearing, language comprehension, object recognition and — medially — memory.

steps.title: Occipital lobe
steps.text: At the back, the occipital lobe contains primary visual cortex.

steps.title: The hidden insula
steps.text: Folded inside the lateral fissure is the insula. We separate the lateral cortex so you can see it.

steps.title: Note on this model
steps.text: In this anatomical asset the inferior frontal gyrus (which includes Broca's area) is not available, so the frontal lobe group contains only the superior, middle and precentral gyri plus the orbital surface.

quiz.q: The primary motor cortex is located in the…
quiz.explain: The precentral gyrus, just in front of the central sulcus, contains primary motor cortex.

quiz.q: Which lobe contains primary visual cortex?
quiz.explain: Primary visual cortex lies along the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe.

modules.title: Exploring the Brainstem
modules.summary: Midbrain, pons and medulla — small structures with vital roles.

steps.title: Brainstem overview
steps.text: The brainstem runs from the diencephalon to the spinal cord. We hide the cerebellum and make the cerebrum transparent.

steps.title: Midbrain
steps.text: The midbrain carries descending motor fibres in the cerebral peduncles and has the superior and inferior colliculi on its back surface for visual and auditory reflexes.

steps.title: Pons
steps.text: The pons links the cerebral cortex with the cerebellum and contains nuclei for facial sensation, facial movement, hearing and balance.

steps.title: Medulla oblongata
steps.text: The medulla contains centres for breathing, heart rate and swallowing, and is where most motor fibres cross to the opposite side.

steps.title: Colliculi from behind
steps.text: Seen from behind, the four colliculi form the tectum of the midbrain.

quiz.q: Which brainstem region contains centres for breathing and swallowing?
quiz.explain: The medulla contains respiratory and swallowing centres.

modules.title: Inside the Limbic System
modules.summary: Hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, fornix and mammillary bodies.

steps.title: A distributed system
steps.text: The 'limbic system' is a set of interconnected structures involved in memory and emotion — not a single anatomical unit.

steps.title: Hippocampus
steps.text: The hippocampus lies in the medial temporal lobe and is essential for forming new episodic memories.

steps.title: Amygdala
steps.text: Just in front of the hippocampus, the amygdala helps attach emotional significance to experiences.

steps.title: Fornix and mammillary bodies
steps.text: The fornix carries hippocampal output in an arch to the mammillary bodies — part of the Papez circuit.

steps.title: Cingulate gyrus
steps.text: The cingulate gyrus arches around the corpus callosum on the medial surface.

quiz.q: The main output pathway of the hippocampus is the…
quiz.explain: Hippocampal output travels through the fornix.

modules.title: Memory and the Hippocampus
modules.summary: How medial temporal structures support memory, and what happens when they are damaged.

steps.title: Finding the hippocampus
steps.text: The hippocampus is internal: we separate the temporal lobes to reveal it.

steps.title: The entorhinal gateway
steps.text: Cortical information reaches the hippocampus mainly through entorhinal cortex in the anterior parahippocampal gyrus.

steps.title: Clinical connections
steps.text: Hippocampal involvement occurs in Alzheimer's disease, temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis and hypoxic-ischaemic injury — by different mechanisms and to different degrees.

options: The hippocampus is essential for forming new episodic memories but memory relies on wider networks
All memories are stored only in the hippocampus
The hippocampus is part of the cerebellum
quiz.explain: Memory depends on distributed networks; the hippocampus is critical for forming new episodic memories.

modules.title: Understanding the Cerebellum
modules.summary: The 'little brain' and its role in coordination.

steps.title: Position
steps.text: The cerebellum sits below the occipital lobes and behind the brainstem.

steps.title: Connections
steps.text: It connects to the brainstem through three pairs of peduncles: to the midbrain, pons and medulla.

steps.title: Lift it away
steps.text: In the Anatomy Lab you can drag the cerebellum away using Manual Dissection mode to see the fourth ventricle in front of it.

steps.title: Model limitation
steps.text: In this asset the cerebellum is one piece: the vermis and hemispheres cannot be selected separately.

quiz.q: A lesion of the left cerebellar hemisphere typically causes clumsiness of the…
quiz.explain: Cerebellar hemispheres coordinate the same side of the body.

modules.title: Brain Structures Involved in Movement
modules.summary: Motor cortex, basal nuclei, thalamus, cerebellum and descending pathways.

steps.title: Primary motor cortex
steps.text: Voluntary movement commands originate largely in the precentral gyrus.

steps.title: Descending pathway
steps.text: Motor fibres descend through the internal capsule and cerebral peduncles into the brainstem.

steps.title: Basal nuclei loop
steps.text: The caudate, putamen and globus pallidus form loops with cortex and thalamus that help select and scale movements.

steps.title: Cerebellar loop
steps.text: The cerebellum compares intended and actual movement and sends corrections to motor cortex via the thalamus.

quiz.q: Which structure relays both basal ganglia and cerebellar output to motor cortex?
quiz.explain: Ventral thalamic nuclei relay these outputs to cortex.

modules.title: Brain Anatomy and Alzheimer's Disease
modules.summary: Typical regional involvement in Alzheimer's disease, explained schematically.

steps.title: Early involvement
steps.text: Tau pathology typically begins in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus. This is a generalised educational pattern, not a patient scan.

steps.title: Spread to association cortex
steps.text: As the disease progresses, temporal and parietal association cortex, the precuneus and posterior cingulate become involved.

steps.title: Relatively spared areas
steps.text: Primary motor, sensory and visual cortices are typically affected late, which is why movement and vision are often preserved early.

quiz.q: Which region is typically involved earliest in Alzheimer's disease?
quiz.explain: Medial temporal structures are typically affected early.

modules.title: Understanding Stroke
modules.summary: Vascular territories and how location shapes stroke symptoms.

steps.title: MCA territory (schematic)
steps.text: The middle cerebral artery supplies much of the lateral frontal, parietal and temporal cortex, the insula and, through deep branches, the basal nuclei and internal capsule. Vessels are not modelled; regions are shown schematically.

steps.title: Deep structures
steps.text: Small deep (lacunar) infarcts in the internal capsule or basal nuclei can cause marked weakness.

steps.title: Posterior circulation
steps.text: Posterior circulation strokes can affect the occipital lobes, thalamus, brainstem and cerebellum.

steps.title: Act fast
steps.text: Sudden face drooping, arm weakness or speech difficulty is an emergency — call emergency services. This app cannot diagnose a stroke.

quiz.q: A stroke in the left occipital lobe most typically causes…
options: Loss of the right visual field in both eyes
quiz.explain: Each occipital lobe processes the opposite visual field.

steps.title: Selective vulnerability
steps.text: Neurodegenerative diseases affect particular neuron populations first. The pattern of early involvement explains early symptoms.

steps.title: Alzheimer's disease
steps.text: Medial temporal and association cortex.

steps.title: Parkinson's disease
steps.text: Substantia nigra (within the cerebral peduncle region — not separately segmented) and its striatal targets.

steps.title: Huntington's disease
steps.text: Striatum — especially the caudate nucleus.

steps.title: ALS
steps.text: Upper motor neurons in the precentral gyrus and lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord.

quiz.q: Which disease most characteristically causes caudate atrophy?
quiz.explain: Striatal (especially caudate) degeneration is central to Huntington's disease.
